hero.title: File:Arnwine-cabin-tn1.jpg
hero.description: Arnwine Cabin at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, in the U.S. state of Tennessee.  This one-room cabin was built by Wes Arnwine in the early 1800s, and used by various descendants until 1936.  The cabin was originally located along the Clinch River near Liberty Hill in Grainger County, Tennessee.  It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.

gallery.title: File:Tom-cassidy-house-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Tom Cassidy's house at the Museum of Appalachian in Norris, Tennessee, USA. Cassidy (1920-1989), who lived in this tiny house until his death, said that it and a few furnishings were all he needed.  The house was originally located near Beard Valley in Union County, Tennessee, and moved to the museum in 2007.

gallery.title: File:Jail-cells-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Late 19th-century jail cells on display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Built in 1874, the cells were 6ft x 9ft and each housed 4 inmates.  They were originally located in Madisonville, Tennessee.

gallery.title: File:Peoples-building-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The People's Building at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This building, built of old hand-made bricks, houses an exhibit of cross maker Harrison Mayes and a collection by folk artist James Bunch.
categories: Folk art museums in the United States

gallery.title: File:Hagood-leather-shop-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Leather and saddle shop at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA. This building, originally located in Persia, Tennessee (a small community at the base of Bays Mountain south of Rogersville), was used by saddle maker Hobart Hagood (d. 1961), and houses his original tools and equipment.

gallery.title: File:Bunch-smokehouse-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Bunch Smokehouse at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The smokehouse was originally located near the Liberty Hill community in Grainger County, Tennessee.

gallery.title: File:General-bunch-house-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The General Bunch House at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA. This house, originally located in the New River section of Anderson County, Tennessee, was built by Pryor Bunch (1852-1931) and family around 1898.  Museum founder John Rice Irwin obtained the cabin from Pryor's son, General, in the 1960s.

gallery.title: File:Mcclung-house-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The McClung House at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Originally located on what is now Kingston Pike a few miles southwest of Knoxville, Tennessee, the house is believed to have been built in the 1790s by the McClung family, who were instrumental in the founding of Knoxville.

gallery.title: File:Broom-and-rope-house-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The broom and rope house at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This structure was originally located at the Mary Carter place in Clinchport, Virginia.  The equipment inside the building belonged to Jim Dagley, who lived a few miles north of the museum.

gallery.title: File:Dan'l-boone-cabin-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The "Dan'l Boone" Cabin at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The cabin was originally located near the Rosedale community in the New River section of Anderson County, Tennessee, and built in the early 19th century.  The cabin's current name comes from its use in the 20th Century Fox TV series, Young Dan'l Boone.

gallery.title: File:Loom-house-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The loom house at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This building, used for spinning and weaving, was originally located on the Bishop Hatmaker estate in Raccoon Valley, Tennessee, just west of Maynardville.  It's part of the museum's "Old Homestead" display.

gallery.title: File:Gwen-sharp-playhouse-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Gwen Sharp's playhouse at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Built in 1929 by a neighbor of Gwen Sharp (b. 1924), this children's playhouse is believed to be the last surviving intact structure from the now-defunct community of Loyston, Tennessee, once located north of modern Big Ridge State Park in Union County.  Loyston was completely submerged by the construction of Norris Reservoir in the 1930s.  Sharp, who was five years old when the playhouse was built, donated it to the museum in 2008.

gallery.title: File:Peters-house-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The Peters House at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This house, originally located near Lutrell, Tennessee, was built in the first half of the 19th century.  Its first known occupant was Nathaniel Peters, who was living in the cabin by about 1840. The cabin, however, may have been built by Nathaniel's father, John, as early as the 1790s. The house is part of the museum's "Old Homestead" display.

gallery.title: File:Parkey-blacksmith-shop-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Parkey Blacksmith Shop at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This structure, originally located in Rebel Hollow (in the Newman's Ridge area of Hancock County, Tennessee), was sold to the museum by the widow of Bill Parkey.

gallery.title: File:Joe-diehl-sawmill-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The Joe Diehl sawmill at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  A roller is ready to feed a log into the blade.

gallery.title: File:Cantilever-barn-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Cantilever (or "Overhang") barn at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This barn was originally located near Seymour, Tennessee.  The Appalachian cantilever barn, derived from similar European barn designs, is rarely found in the United States outside the mountains of East Tennessee.

gallery.title: File:Wilson-barn-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The Wilson barn at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA. Allen Noble describes this type of barn as a side drive crib barn.  A peacock is in the foreground.

gallery.title: File:Whiskey-still-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Whiskey still at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The still was moved to the museum in the 1990s and was set up at the present site by famed moonshiner Marvin "Popcorn" Sutton (1946-2009), who provided a few of the components.

gallery.title: File:Museum of Appalachia.jpg
gallery.description: Cantilever Barn and Hacker Martin Grist Mill at the Museum of Appalachia.

gallery.title: File:Cowbells-museumofappalachia2.jpg
gallery.description: A display of cow bellss (and sheep bells in bottom row) formerly used by Appalachian farmers, collected by John Rice Irwin. Photo taken at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, United States, summer 1998. Self-made photo.

gallery.title: File:Monroe-kitchen-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The Mark Monroe Pioneer Log Kitchen at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This kitchen, originally located in Maynardville, Tennessee, was eventually converted into a smokehouse by the Monroes.

gallery.title: File:Honey-bee-tree-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Tree trunk used to attract honey bees at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA. Trunk is of a dead Eastern Juniper (Juniperus virginiana), mislabelled "cedar" (Cedrus). This tree was once located in Friendsville, Tennessee.

gallery.title: File:Murder-banjo-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: The "murder banjo" at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The banjo was owned by an African-American banjo player named Henry Dobson in the latter half of the 19th century.  One night around 1895, Dobson was playing along the Allegheny River in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania when a fight erupted and his closest friend was knifed to death, splattering blood all over the banjo.  Dobson refused to play it again, and eventually traded it to Charles Ross Schrecengost for a guitar.  Museum founder John Rice Irwin obtained the banjo from Schrecengost's son, Haven (a resident of Grainger County, Tennessee) in 1989.  Dobson's name is inscribed on the banjo in two places, with the dates 1878 and 1881.

gallery.title: File:Banjos-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Display of banjos from around the Appalachian region at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This display is in the "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building near the museum entrance.

gallery.title: File:John-maxwell-dulcimers-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Collection of Appalachian dulcimers (sometimes called "fretted" or "mountain" dulcimers) on display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  These dulcimers were designed by dulcimer maker John Maxwell.  This display is in the museum's "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building near the museum entrance.  The Appalachian dulcimer is a type of zither, and shouldn't be confused with the hammered dulcimer.

gallery.title: File:Peacock-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: One of several peacocks that freely roam the grounds of the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.

gallery.title: File:Slave-cabin-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Slave cabin on display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The cabin was originally located on the Merritt family lands in Grainger County, Tennessee, and was probably built by Sam Merritt around 1820.

gallery.title: File:Fred-stone-medical-bag-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Medical bag used by Dr. Fred Stone, Sr., who operated out of the NRHP-listed Dr. Fred Stone, Sr. Hospital, on display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This display is located on the second floor of the "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building.

gallery.title: File:Fred-stone-security-badge-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Oak Ridge security badge of Dr. Fred Stone, Sr., on display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Oak Ridge's Manhattan Project installations, which helped build the world's first atomic bomb in the 1940s, were known to the public as the "Clinton Engineer Works."  Stone examined new employees of the Stone and Webster Construction Company, which built many of the project's facilities.  This badge is on display on the second floor of the museum's "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building.

gallery.title: File:Fred-stone-stethoscope-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Early-20th century stethoscope used by Dr. Fred Stone, Sr., who operated out of his NRHP-listed hospital in Oliver Springs, Tennessee, USA, in the 1950s and 1960s.  This stethoscope is on display on the second floor of the "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.

gallery.title: File:Fred-stone-display-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Dr. Fred Stone, Sr. display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  This display is part of the museum's country doctors and dentists section located on the second floor of the museum's "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building.  The top-left section of the display shows Stone's medical bag, stethoscope, Oak Ridge security badge, the sign that hung above the doors of his Oliver Springs hospital, and several photographs.  The lower-left section is dedicated to Stone's grandfather, Dr. Samuel Stone of Claiborne County.  The middle section displays historic photographs and information.  The right section shows Stone's World War I-era hats (top), Stone's Lincoln Memorial University diploma, Stone's British Military Cross citation, and several historic photographs.  The boots on the lower right were Stone's English horse-riding boots.

gallery.title: File:Cas-walker-bust-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Bust of Cas Walker at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Walker was a well-known East Tennessee businessman and politician.

gallery.title: File:Cas-walker-display-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Cas Walker display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  Walker was a well-known East Tennessee businessman and politician.  This display is located on the first floor of the "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building.

gallery.title: File:Uncle-dave-macon-display-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Uncle Dave Macon display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The display shows some of Macon's furniture and a guitar once owned by his son, Dorris.  This display is located on the first floor of the museum's "Appalachian Hall of Fame" building.

gallery.title: File:Tennessee-ramblers-display-moa-tn1.jpg
gallery.description: Tennessee Ramblers display at the Museum of Appalachia in Norris, Tennessee, USA.  The Tennessee Ramblers, created by "Fiddlin' Bill Sievers" and his children, Mack and Willie, played old-time and hawaiian music in the Knoxville area for nearly of half-century.  The display shows Bill Sievers' fiddle and a 1940s-era advertisement.
